utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case. And could, meanwhile, the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Marcus, perhaps a question: Were you able to digest, more or less, the material which you initially said were 85 pages and then a few hundred pages?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have had -- I've had a team of people working on it. It seems to me -- and I will know before the end of my cross-examination, it seems to me that it might be okay, in other words that we might not need to, but I'm just waiting for that absolute final confirmation. I'm quite optimistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, because you needed two sessions today, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you were on your feet but not anymore. May I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Peremptory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Bosnic, I'd like to remind you -- can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm always inclined also to say "dobro jutro," but then of course we do not know whether the translation is functioning. Mr. Bosnic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Ms. Marcus will now continue her cross-examination. Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bosnic.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your statement, you said that at meetings you did in fact discuss asking the federal government for political support but you did not discuss asking them for weapons. Then you state that you know that Babic went to Belgrade at the end of 1990 and beginning of 1991 and discussed the possibility of them providing economical support. Do you know the details of these conversations which Babic had in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of financial support they were discussing?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were discussing monetary assistance, and the linking of federal organs with the municipal organs because Croatia had stopped subsidizing the municipalities there, so we wanted it to be made possible for us to pay the municipal taxes into the federal budget and in that way for resources to be returned to the areas of the municipalities in question. We also wanted enterprises and firms from those municipalities if they were not in contact with enterprises in the rest of Yugoslavia to link -- be linked with them and start co-operating with them, because co-operation with firms, with enterprises in the area of Croatia, had been severed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up P1101. This is a public document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, the document you're going to see now on the screen in front of you was shown to you prior to coming to Court and you provided some comments on your comments chart in relation to this document, which is P1101. What you say about the document in your chart is that: "It was a strategy of political leaders of SAO Krajina to request assistance from the Republic of Serbia, as it would be difficult to explain to the Serbian people in Serbia if they denied these requests." My question to you is: How many such requests for assistance from Serbia are you aware of?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say the exact number now, but the idea was in those crisis moments for us to turn to Serbia for assistance, because the citizens of Serbia could see that they were having a very hard time, especially after the raid of Petrinja, the incursion into Petrinja in September 1990, or October, I'm not quite sure, when Special Police forces raided the place and over 150 people were arrested. That was the first incident. From that moment on we started discussing in what way we would be able to protect us from incursions by Special Police Units, and this was -- that was the concrete cause of this particular raid by Croatian special units, i.e., forces in Plitvice. We could then see that our police and our village guards were simply unable to withstand, to resist, the Croatian Special Police forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was it an effective strategy, this strategy of requesting assistance from the Republic of Serbia? Was it effective?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, no. But later it became evident that there were certain results, that some headway had been made. This training camp was set up and subsequently through the federal organs or, more specifically, the federal Secretariat of National Defence, at the request of Mr. Babic, schooled officers started arriving, retired officers who hailed from the Krajina. They came to our Territorial Defence zone staffs in order to assist us as professionals. And later when the JNA barracks were surrounded, when the water-supply was cut off, et cetera, the JNA also became involved in dealing with these problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, I have quite a lot of material to cover. I'm going to ask you respectfully to limit your answers. And if we need further clarification, we will ask you. Now, during your testimony you spoke about a meeting between Babic and Milosevic which Babic told you about afterwards. You said: "Milan Babic went to Belgrade for discussions with Slobodan Milosevic. While in Belgrade, he placed a call to the party head office asking that an Assembly be convened which was supposed to be the constituent Assembly of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina."

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is this the same meeting or a different meeting than the one you just described before?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these events took place later. That was December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: How many of these meetings in Belgrade did you attend with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximation? Was it one or two, ten or twenty, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say five or six. I attended five or six meetings, but I was often with Babic in Belgrade on other business.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And over what period of time would you say those five or six meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately from November 1991 to 1994 or 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any meeting involving Milan Babic, Milan Martic, and Jovica Stanisic in a cafe between Knin and Golubic at the end of August 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any meeting involving Milan Babic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, and Jovica Stanisic in Belgrade in January of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any meeting involving Slobodan Milosevic, Radmilo Bogdanovic, Milan Babic, and Jovica Stanisic in Belgrade at President Milosevic's office at the end of March 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So I take it you are also not aware of a meeting between Milan Babic, Jovica Stanisic, and Franko Simatovic in Babic's apartment in Knin in April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What about a meeting between Milan Babic, Dusan Orlovic, Milan Martic, and Jovica Stanisic in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you concede that it is possible that Babic might not have informed you of his ties with Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible, but it would have been surprising, in fact, incredible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, a couple of times in your statement you speak about humanitarian funds. What do you mean when you say "humanitarian funds"?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean food supplies, clothing, footwear, medical supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are these supplies for the military or for the population, generally, or for the police?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities requested this for the civilian population and through the Territorial Defence for the requirements of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, are you familiar with someone named Dusan Momcilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution's case is that Mr. Dusan Momcilovic was sent by the Serbian DB to the RSK. Were you familiar with other individuals sent by the Serbian DB as volunteers to the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know them. I never met them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please call up 65 ter 6227.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, what I'm showing you are a couple of pages from this person Dusan Momcilovic's Serbian DB personnel file.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have been up on my feet more quickly, but there's an objection to the use of this document, based on the Prlic appeal decision, which I'd like to argue, if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one you gave us yesterday or one of these days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, we do have copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you distributed copies already, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there's no need to do it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Whilst that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've read that. How much time would you need for that? Do we -- should we do it in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, could I ask that the document be removed from the screen, please, until we deal with this issue, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for my recollection, I remember that the decision on a specific document was not the subject of an appeal, it was, rather, the general approach, the ruling on how to, in more general terms. And from what I remember, but I'm summarising now perhaps too much, is that the Appeals Chamber said that there was no legal error in the decision made and that these kind of decisions could be made, as was also emphasised by the Trial Chamber, I think, on a case-by-case basis, but under this general guidance which was not in violation of any rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that sums it -- the situation. In principle, and this is the position we've been advancing since the beginning of the Defence case, that in principle there is nothing wrong with allowing the Prosecution or party to admit documents after the close of their case, but under certain threshold conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And obviously the more that is sought to be done by the Prosecution, the more the concern must arise. The starting point being that the Prosecution must serve their case before the beginning of it, except under certain limited circumstances. In fact, one could argue that most of the interlocutory jurisprudence is premised on that simple fact. And the Prosecution must know their case, they must serve it at the beginning of it, and then there are various ways in which exceptions are made, whether additional evidence or additional witnesses, so on and so forth. But as the Prlic Appeal Chamber makes clear, the Prosecution can add to their case only in exceptional circumstances. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, if -- I think the Appeals Chamber said that if you -- if a Chamber takes as a -- as a general line that it can be done only in exceptional circumstances, that that doesn't show any error in law. But let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's precisely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is not exactly the same as what you said. And that has got something to do with the role of an appellate authority. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I don't understand the distinction that Your Honour makes and I'd like to understand it so I can address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a Chamber adopts a position that something can be done only in exceptional circumstances, and if that position is that decision is not quashed as showing any legal error, that does not automatically yet mean that the exceptional circumstances are always required by the appellate authority. The review is not a hundred per cent a full one on appeal on these kind of matters. But we'll reread it anyhow --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that your argument's too sophisticated for me. I don't quite grasp it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's -- or it could be wrong as well, or not clear. Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I think I understand Your Honour's point. It's in paragraph 24 of the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't have it here but I have it on my desk, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where it notes the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that this careful approach, establishing a high threshold for the admission of fresh evidence, duly mindful of Rules 89(C) and (D) of the rules, may be justified depending on the specific circumstances of the case. I mean, to summarise: In principle, the Prosecution can do it, but it comes with dangers, and the principal danger is that the accused has a fundamental right to know the case that he must meet. And the more that a party is allowed to make inroads into that, the more the Prosecution are allowed to make inroads into that, the more dangers there are to that fundamental right. And my learned friend is sitting on a file with, I think, ten new documents for one single witness. I think we counted recently and we're already into the double figures of new documents introduced during the Prosecution case. At this rate we will be well into the hundreds by the end of the Defence case. And in our respectful submission that's why the threshold criteria at this stage must be applied as strictly as possible and that's why the Prosecution must justify their position and justify why they are seeking to make inroads into a fundamental right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Any specifics about this document? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we -- you were talking about quantity; of course quality may play a role in every single decision as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would answer it in this way: First of all, the Prosecution are in possession of thousands of documents in B/C/S and what they're doing is they're using their vast resources to sit and sift through that material, pick out what they think is useful, and then use it against the accused, knowing full well the Defence does not have the resources to go through those thousands of documents, knowing full well we do not have the language resources to do that, knowing full well that is a breach of Rule 66, to be using -- and this is the real problem here. Rule 66 requires them to serve the evidence that they rely upon at a certain time, but also in a certain form: in English. What the Prosecution are doing is simply drawing on their vast database, which is in B/C/S, at the last minute disclosing it to the Defence in English, at a time where we cannot possibly go through our database and look to contextualise the evidence that they're seeking now to add in the case. It's, in short, it's a trial by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but are you -- I asked you whether you had any specifics for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's the general objection we have to the approach. In relation to the specific objection, I don't know what the Prosecution want to do with this document and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can only formulate a specific objection when the Prosecution indicate what is the document, what do they say is its probative value, why do they say they should be allowed to use it at this stage, why didn't they use it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prlic Appeals Chamber decision circulated by the Stanisic Defence sets out certain guiding principles in relation to the presentation of evidence by the Prosecution in cross-examination where this evidence has not been presented during the Prosecution's case in chief. According to the Prlic decision, the Chamber has discretion to admit fresh evidence under Rules 89(C) and (D), taking into account the probative value of the evidence and the need to ensure a fair trial. The Chamber can consider, in seeking to strike this balance, the mode of disclosure, the purpose of admission, and any other factual considerations. As you are aware, Your Honours, and as Mr. Jordash has said, the Prosecution is in possession of hundreds of DB personnel files which were received at different times and always pursuant to an RFA to the Serbian authorities. These personnel files have all been disclosed to the Defence, some several times. The personnel files are all relevant to this case. However, the Prosecution made selections of personnel files or documents from personnel files to tender in its case in chief, some through bar table motions and some through witnesses. We stand by that selection and in our view we met our burden in our case in chief by the tendering of the personnel files and documents from those files which we chose. Now the Defence case is being presented and the Defence witnesses are bringing their evidence. The Prosecution is responding and challenging the evidence of these witnesses. It is the choice of the Defence to bring the witnesses they bring. And if the witnesses present certain evidence, other evidence relevant to the Prosecution case and directly contradicting the evidence of Defence witnesses will be selected for use in cross-examination of those witnesses. If the Defence brings evidence that there was no DB involvement in the Krajina, the Prosecution must be permitted to put to the Defence witness evidence of DB involvement in the Krajina, and to select evidence which is particularly within the area of familiarity of that witness. Dusan Momcilovic was a DB operative since 1991 who held positions in Glina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- just before you proceed, is this to be presented in the presence of the witness? Or I'm also looking at -- or should we ask the witness just to -- if you go into much detail, then of course it might not be wise to do that in the presence of the witness and then ask him questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave out the part about this particular document then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you say but it's relevant in this context and this witness could -- would know about --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Directly relevant to this witness's evidence, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just a few more general points on the submission made by Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Defence has themselves conceded the relevance of the personnel files. They tendered the personnel file of JF-048, they tendered a photograph from the personnel file of another individual as D261, they uploaded one other whole file - I'll leave out the names for now - as 2D268, and other entire file as 2D269, although they did not tender those whole files. In the course of the beginning of the Defence case, the Defence has dropped their objections to P179 and P473, both personnel files. And following objections to yet another personnel file, just last week or the week before perhaps, the Defence decided to drop its objections and seek the tendering of the entire personnel file when I had tendered only a portion of it. Many of the personnel files contain similar documents and the parties and the Chamber have no doubt become increasingly familiar with these documents and the contents. The Defence appears to have come to the conclusion that at least in certain instances the personnel files are relevant to their case as well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please read more slowly for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you. This is evident from the recent dropping of objections by the Defence. Now, Your Honours, as the Defence witnesses testify, other portions of personnel files or, in fact, of other documents in the possession of the Prosecution will become relevant specifically to the evidence presented by those witnesses. The Prosecution would like to avoid lengthy debates in court about the admissibility of these documents. Of course, it's always open to the Defence to generally concede the relevance to the truth-seeking process of the DB personnel files, for example, as a category, rather than making heated objections only to drop them later. Finally, with respect to this witness in particular, Your Honour, the Defence has stated that due to the dropping of another witness who could give evidence -- who could give evidence in relation to the Krajina, they wanted to add additional areas of examination of this witness. We did not object on grounds of lack of notice. Our submission is that this has opened the door even wider with respect to this witness and the Prosecution cannot now be disabled in its ability to put to this witness evidence which is directly relevant to his testimony, including in its expanded form. I've noticed, yes, approximately ten documents to put to this witness. These are non-admitted, say, fresh evidence documents, many of which come from personnel files, some of which come from RFA responses. All of which, I submit, meet the requirements under the rules of relevance and probative value and all of which are now being specifically tendered as a direct result of the evidence presented by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I give you the opportunity, Mr. Jordash, to briefly respond, I already make one observation. Sometimes I think your objections did not stand but mainly because the document was in part admitted and then you said, Okay, but then I'd like to have the whole document in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear that's not true for all of them, but that's -- I noticed this already so that that's on my mind. Any other brief comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And of course there will be circumstances where the Prosecution wish to admit document and we don't object to it because we're not taking the position that the Prosecution should never be allowed to introduce new evidence. That's obviously not the position taken by the Prlic Appeal Chamber and it's not a position which is founded, we submit, in common sense. But nonetheless, there ought to be a process by which these issues are decided, and the process does not begin and end with relevance. With an indictment such as this, many, many, many things could be relevant. That simply cannot be the only threshold criteria because then we move from a trial into a truth and reconciliation commission. And I note that my learned friend's submission has not once mentioned the right to be informed of the nature and cause of the charges. For the Prosecution it's about relevance to what they say is a truth-finding process. Well, as Your Honours know, this is a trial, and that comes with certain procedural guarantees and certain procedural regularities. That is all we're requesting here, that the Prosecution meet those procedural threshold criteria as indicated by the Prlic Appeal Chamber. Those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber denies the objection as made in relation to the document presented. The Chamber will very likely come with a broader guidance relatively soon. And up until that moment we'll decide, of course, on any fresh evidence presented by the Prosecution. Also, in view of the broader guidance with the reasons for that to be given, the Chamber refers already now for the reasons why it denied the objection. There is another matter, I think in the Prlic decision also it's required to tell the parties for what purpose the evidence is admitted. I think it would be here not to impeach the witness but, rather, to present to the witness, also for the truth of the contents, certain material so that he can -- he can reconsider perhaps whether he can refresh his memory or further consider whether he has any comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just add for the record, and in no way am I seeking to go behind Your Honours's ruling, but I have never heard -- and I've consulted with my team, I've never heard of Dusan Momcilovic being part of the Prosecution case. I have no idea what that is about. We've looked at disclosure in the time that we've had, and we don't know. But I put that on the record. And as I say, I don't go behind Your Honours' ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Marcus, you may proceed. And perhaps the last observation by Mr. Jordash you would keep that in mind also for any other evidence you may wish to present as fresh evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think Your Honours will see the evidence that we have presented with respect to this individual. Now, could I please have again, and perhaps it should not be broadcast to the public, 65 ter 6227. Can I suggest that maybe we just expanded the B/C/S, the original. It's legible if it's expanded, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bosnic, what you see before you is a document from the personnel file of a man named Dusan Momcilovic. What I'm going to do is show you a few entries from this file and then I'll ask you a few questions about what we have seen. On this page I'd like to call your attention to where it says that Dusan Momcilovic was employed in the MUP of the Republic of Serbia from August 1991 into 1994. Do you see what I'm referring to on the left side of the page?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer now please turn to page 2. And maybe in this case we can also have the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see before you is the biography written by Dusan Momcilovic himself. If you look at the third paragraph, you will see that he says that from 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I just may briefly interrupt you. Could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, when you called for this document the first time, it was shown to the public, which it should not. Now, we go into the content of this document and usually these personnel files are confidential because it would reveal who worked for the service, and they may still be working for the service. So therefore, just not showing the document and then ask all the questions with the names and functions would not provide the protection which is granted, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, if you would please put those questions in private session to the witness and we'll try to see whether the first showing on the screen can be made -- can be undone. Madam Registrar is working on that. I would like now to proceed. If everyone has finished his -- on all sides of the room their consultations, then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I've just been informed, Your Honour, that this was already redacted. In other words, that the redactions were the proposed protected measures on the document, but Ms. Friedman is going to confirm that for me and then we can come back to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if you look, Mr. Bosnic, at this biography written by Dusan Momcilovic, you will see that he was -- he says that from 1991 he was a member of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, RDB, JSO, employed in the field in the "Krajina" as a member of the Glina SUP from 1991 to 1993; commander of the 24th Brigade of the VRS in 1994 to 1995; and in 1995 he was the commander of the special unit of the RSK MUP. One last page before I put my questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could we please turn to page 3. Now, Your Honours, on this page I didn't see any need for it to be submitted for translation, but if Your Honours deem that it should, I will certainly do so. I'd like to focus on the bottom photograph, bottom entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, you can see this is Dusan Momcilovic's driver's licence and it says MUP of Serbia. Now, my questions to you are as follows:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- it does not only say MUP of Serbia, but it says "Izdate od," and I'd like to know what that means. Perhaps you can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, what does it mean "Izdate od" MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that it was issued to him by the MUP of Serbia. In other words, issued by the MUP of Serbia, in their offices by the body competent to issue driving licences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be my next question, Ms. Marcus, whether the MUP of Serbia is the general authority to issue driving licences to anyone who wants to drive on public roads. Is the MUP of Serbia also issuing driving licences to dentists and greengrocers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To all those who have passed a driving test. They receive a certificate on the basis of which the MUP will issue them with a driving licence. Whether it was the MUP of Serbia or the MUP of Croatia, the procedure was the same for all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the same would be true for policemen, civilians, whomever? Is that how I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please go back to page 2 for my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bosnic, were you aware -- now, I asked you if you knew Dusan Momcilovic, has any of this refreshed your memory of this person named Dusan Momcilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I probably did meet him at some of these meetings, but the photograph does not refresh my memory of him and of meeting him at any given point.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At the meetings that you're talking about where you may have met, but you're not sure, Dusan Momcilovic, were you generally informed of individuals such as Mr. Momcilovic who had a dual employment, who were sent by the Serbian MUP to field operations in the Krajina? Were you aware of such individuals?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that there were such people around. Dusan Momcilovic is from Krajina who came to Glina from Zagreb, and it is true that they would introduce individuals to us at the meetings that I attended, but at no point was anyone introduced as a member of the MUP or the DB and as having been from the area of Krajina. So I mean chief of SUPs, commanders of units, commanders of TOs, of TO units, presidents of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've just been informed by Ms. Friedman that we can use this redacted version, that Dusan Momcilovic's name was not redacted in the proposed redactions by Serbia therefore this can be public and all this testimony that's been in private session, with Your Honours' leave, can be put into public. I'd also like to tender this -- these pages as a public exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would object insofar as on page 1 of this document we can see that it's an excerpt from his work record booklet, but we don't see who the booklet belongs to because we don't see the name. And as a rule, the booklet should also be certified. There is no evidence of that. There is no evidence of who the booklet belongs to. And whomever it may belong to, it has not been certified and stamped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we object for the same reasons and also for lack of notice reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Specifically on -- I mean, the lack of notice, that is clear. That's on the basis of your previous submissions. Now, authenticity and insufficient indicia of -- could you please respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We -- this -- these are pages from this individual's DB personnel file that we received from the DB. I'm perfectly happy to go through this and see what other pages are in there and to show them perhaps informally to Mr. Petrovic so that he can maybe see the stamp. Perhaps we have a better copy of it, et cetera. The copy I reviewed before looked more clear than the one that we saw here on the screen. So I'm happy to deal with that out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apart from how clear the copy is, what we see on the first page of this document are pages 7 and 8 of a document. And perhaps it could be matched to the biography. I have not even made an attempt to do so. But perhaps it would be good if you look again at the material you received and that it will be marked for identification first, because if these documents are three pages from a file, then, of course, if it is not a complete file, then it should at least be established that all the pages relate to the same person. And that's, as far as I can see, not yet the case for the first page, being pages 7 and 8 of the booklet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will look for that and then we will propose -- perhaps discuss with the Defence whether more pages should be tendered and propose to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number for this document to be MFI'd would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P2995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, in your statement in paragraph 45 you talk about humanitarian help. This was what I meant to ask you -- this is what I was referring to earlier. I'll read you one line. It says one part -- perhaps I would go back a line for the context: "At this time the general budgets were coming from the income of the municipalities. One part of this was coming from the federal government as humanitarian help for the Krajina. This help was received up until the time I was in the government, which was in 1994. I do not know how much this was in 1991. In November 1991, this amounted to 15 per cent of the total budget of the SAO Krajina." In the next paragraph, in paragraph 46, you say: "The aid provided by the federal government was also used to pay for salaries and other things, in Kordun and Banija, this was from late 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could the witness be shown the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's D313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And while we are waiting, Ms. Marcus, in view of the questions that were put in relations to the pages 2 and 3 of the document, I think it would be necessary to have a translation of -- especially of page 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour. Thank you. So I'm referring -- oh, Your Honours, can we turn to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We return into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bosnic, what -- I'll ask you again, then: The use of the term humanitarian help is the one I'd like you to clarify. You said earlier that what you meant was supplies for the civilians, but in paragraphs 45 and 46 it appears you're talking about funding for salaries, and I'd like to understand what you mean by "humanitarian help."

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I mean, what I already said, and the other part which was also -- dealt with the budget were financial resources to pay the workers in the health, education, and other sectors which were financed from the budget. Pensioners, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Captain Dragan Fund?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it in Belgrade after we fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that Captain Dragan had set up a fund and was collecting monies, resources, in order to assist wounded fighters from the areas which were gripped by the war and who did not have adequate assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you -- were you aware of individuals applying to the Captain Dragan Fund for financial support?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that they did apply, otherwise the fund would not have had a purpose. I was not a member of that fund nor did I apply for anything from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 6217, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The same objection. We submit the Prosecution must tell us what they're doing, why they're doing it, and why they're doing it so late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, any specifics in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could take off his headphones for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask: Do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I studied German and Russian. I definitely do not understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could you take off your earphones. Yes, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I mentioned earlier, it's the Prosecution's case that Dusan Momcilovic is one example of a DB operative who was functioning in the field in the RSK specifically in the areas and at the time period that this witness is talking about. This is an application to the KDF fund by Dusan Momcilovic. I was planning to show two pages from this document. And then I was planning to show an intercept where Milan Martic and Toso Paic speak about Dusan Momcilovic. And then I was planning on showing the Kula video where Dusan Momcilovic receives an award directly from Mr. Stanisic. So Dusan Momcilovic is one of the unit members in the Kula video who -- now, I was planning to show this to Mr. Bosnic and to demonstrate to him, to see whether he agrees, that there may have been quite a lot of DB involvement, in fact, in the Krajina without him being aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but always about the same personal, if I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Until the Kula video, yes, Your Honour. Up to and including the Kula video, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you can start with the first document. The Kula video, the Chamber is it not yet convinced that that adds anything at this moment, that showing it to the witness would assist us any further. The first document is fine, then we'll see how matters develop, and then we'll decide on the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The mention of the Kula video was also in response to Mr. Jordash's claim that they never heard of Dusan Momcilovic before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but do we need the witness to establish that, or?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, sir, I take your order, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't say I hadn't heard of him before. I said I didn't understand what part he played in the Prosecution case, and I stand by that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bosnic, what you see before you, as I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Oh, perhaps he should put his headphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- Yes, we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What you see before you is a page from an application by this same Dusan Momcilovic to the Captain Dragan Fund that we were just speak being. I'm going to show you two pages from this and then ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please turn to page 2 in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you can see here, Mr. Bosnic, under the section where it says "data on injury" Dusan Momcilovic states that he was commander of the unit of the Special Police Unit for Krajina as of 16th of June, 1991. He took part in the Corridor Operation, he says. Are you familiar with the Corridor Operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, just in one line, what that operation was?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the area around Banja Luka could no longer establish or have physical contact with Serbia. That is why the corridor problem arose, in order to have access to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of other individuals who took part in the corridor operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So am I correct when I ask you -- when I say that your evidence is that you know that people applied to the Captain Dragan Fund for financial support but this is the first time you're seeing an actual application; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I have page 5, please. Your Honours, I was just informed, unfortunately, that the English translation is not yet available for this page. I will certainly only seek its marking for identification from Your Honours. I do apologise for that, and we'll fix that as a matter of urgency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, what you see in front of you is another page from this same application to the Captain Dragan Fund. This page is signed by Djure Ljiljak, secretary of the Glina SUP. Are you familiar with Djure Ljiljak?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last name does ring a bell, and we probably or certainly met at meetings. There was a secretary in the Glina SUP by that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Djure Ljiljak was also a member of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender this, I suppose marked for identification pending the translation of the third page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it objection, the same, Mr. Jordash. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. The number, Madam Registrar, would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be P2996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2996. Please proceed, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I please have 65 ter 6218.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, what is loading on the screen before you is a transcript of an intercepted conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we ask the witness to take his earphones off for a second. Ms. Marcus, what are you going to elicit as evidence in relation to this document from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This is an intercepted conversation between Milan Martic and Toso Paic where the unit commanded by Dusan Momcilovic is described. Now, the witness has given quite a lot of evidence about Milan Martic and Toso Paic. This links Dusan Momcilovic into the -- directly into the evidence that the witness gave, and I'm going to ask him what is the role of the Special Police brigade that Dusan Momcilovic commanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I take it whether he has any knowledge of such a unit, because if he doesn't have that -- why not ask him first these questions before, whether he -- because if he doesn't know anything, then I do not expect that by listening to an intercepted telephone conversation that that will in any way add -- assist him in -- at least unless if you have good reasons to believe that this might really refresh his memory and suddenly everything becomes clear to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I will ask him about his knowledge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's then start with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And perhaps you take off the screen for a moment the document you asked to be shown. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we ask the witness, please, to put back on his ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, are you aware of a Special Police brigade in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And are you aware that this was commanded by Dusan Momcilovic in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to show him the intercept to see if it might refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just would like to make the point that this, the introduction of this document, creates potentially tens and tens of legal hours of work - checking authenticity, calling evidence to challenge authenticity, if that's the result of the preliminary inspection. Trying to meet evidence like this this late in the day is an uphill struggle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my objection differs on what -- from Mr. Jordash's objection. The Defence of Mr. Simatovic tried to present the same type of documents many times during the Prosecution case and the comment of our learned colleague from the Prosecution was that these were documents obtained from Croatia, that they had not been fully authenticated, that they were a retold intercept, in fact. If the Prosecution has changed their position, if they now feel that such a type of document is acceptable and suitable for use in the courtroom and for being tendered as an exhibit, so if they have changed their position, I should like to ask that that be noted and that that also refer to the intercepts that we have proposed and we'll seek to tender in the future and which belong to the same collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At transcript page 12734 on to 12735, Mr. Jordash asked the witness whether he was aware -- whether he might have been -- might have expected to hear about the existence of more than one unit. "Please give a selection of people who you might have expected to hear that from but didn't." The witnesses answer was: "For the area of Kordun, I would certainly have heard it from Milos or Toso Paic, from the commanders of TO staffs, or representatives of the JNA at the meetings I attended." Now, this was -- this, what I was going to put to the witness, was directly in response to that with respect to the Special Police brigade. The witness has now said that he knows about the Special Police brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, no one asked the witness to take his earphones off. Could you also respond to the authenticity concern Mr. Petrovic expressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we received the transcript of this intercepted conversation from the Government of Croatia, but that is the information that I have on the origin of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Petrovic has said that you had objected against documents obtained from Croatia. Now, I do not have a clear recollection on what exactly he is referring to. Is there any -- apart from that you obtained it from Croatia, is there any further evidence on the authenticity and the accuracy of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I don't have any additional information, Your Honours. I would say that this would go to the weight, due to the very clear import and relevance of this document directly to contradict what the witness said. If Mr. Petrovic is referring to the book of documents from Croatia, we objected to a book, not to the underlying documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an entirely different matter. If you were referring to the book which presents the number -- but that's not what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, I did not refer -- I was not referring to the book. It is a document of the same type from the same collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is granted. You may proceed, Ms. Marcus. Well, let's have a look at the clock. It's time for a break, approximately. There is one issue I would very briefly like to put on the record. P2993 was assigned twice, first to 65 ter 1441 which was tendered by the Prosecution through Witness DST-034 on the 7th of July, and then again to 65 ter 6216 which was marked in court by Witness DST-034 on the 11th of July. Therefore, the second document I mentioned needs another number to be assigned to it. 6216, a document marked in court by Witness DST-034 on the 11th of July and saved as IC00-0032 now receives the new number P2994, and that also explains why Madam Registrar today started assigning new numbers 2995. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, are you ready and are you still on schedule?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I was informed that the time that I've used thus far is one hour and 30 minutes -- just one hour. Okay. I'm going to do my best, Your Honour. I have cut quite a lot. I will do my very best. It may be that I have to go somewhat into the third session. I'm very conscious of the witness's limitation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, have you had an opportunity to think of the names of any other individuals who are deployed from Kordun to Golubic for training either in the first group or in the group which stayed behind to continue the training?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you some of the names. I'm very glad that you hold me in such high esteem, actually, that you believe that I have the capacity of recalling many things and events that transpired from 1990 up to this point in time. I have recalled all the names that I could, so that I believe any further effort on my part would be an exercise in futility. I've told you all the names that I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, we are short in time. So if you would have said "I do not remember any other names than I gave already," that is one line; whereas now it is ten lines. Could you please try to assist us also in taking care that you will be able to leave in time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraphs 58 and 59, you describe the training at Golubic under Captain Dragan. In paragraph 56 you state that after the first group was trained in Golubic, part of that group remained at Golubic to continue to train others. You say: "This group was known as the Knindzes and became a special unit of the police." You then say that members of the Knindzes participated in an operation in Glina in 1991. Were you present at the planning meetings prior to the deployment of the Knindzes to the Glina operation?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your statement lists the date at September 1991. The information we have is that it was in July 1991. Is that -- can you comment on the month?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was actually the end of July 1991. The last week of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So we'll take that as a correction to your statement to the noting of September; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that is what I stated in the statement, then, yes, this is a correction. I mixed up the dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript 12729 to 12730 you were asked: "Did Captain Dragan, as is claimed here, have units, in the plural, or just a unit, as far as you're concerned, as far as you were aware?" Your answer was: "As far as I'm aware, Captain Dragan had just this one unit which was called the Knindzes and which had specific patches, the Serbian coat of arms with the four Ss turned upside down or in the other -- facing the other direction from the regular one." You then were asked by Judge Orie: "How do you know about their patches?" Your answer was: "I never saw them in action, but these men who completed their training and returned to the area of Kordun wore the uniforms of the Krajina milicija. And I saw Captain Dragan in Knin and I also saw a man by the name [sic] of Cigo and I saw the commander of the armoured train, his name was Blagoje Guska, and they wore these uniforms and they had red berets." Mr. Bosnic, were you aware that Nikola Simic, aka Cigo or Ciga, participated in the operation in Glina?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've just reminded me of his last name. I knew him as Cigo. I don't know that he participated in that action.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Would the Court Officer please call up Exhibit P2875.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, what you're going to see is a report written by Nikola Simic, also known as Cigo, as you say, about the operation in Glina. Now if I could call your attention to the top of the page. You see the heading on the report says "The Special Purposes Unit of the Republic of the Serbia SAO Krajina." Do you know if this was the special purposes unit you referred to earlier as the Special Police Unit or the Knindzes?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cigo was in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: As you can see here in the first line, Nikola Simic says he was stationed in Glina with the special unit. Could I draw your attention to a bit further down the page where it mentioned someone named Sasa Medakovic. Do you know Sasa Medakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 6230, please, and could it -- well, perhaps in an abundance of caution we should move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, in paragraph 25 of your statement you state that you put pressure on Toso Paic to accept Milan Martic. In your testimony before this Chamber, you said that you were the one to suggest Toso Paic to Milan Babic as his deputy for Kordun in February 1992. Were you aware that Toso Paic was an advisor to the Serbian DB chief in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about what Toso Paic's role was prior to February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know from the field is that he was one of the heads of the police in Kordun. From my conversations with him and Milos Pajic, I know that previously he had worked in our representation offices in France and, I believe, in New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was it about Toso Paic that Milos Pajic said which convinced you to support Toso Paic's candidacy?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to propose Milos Pajic, who told me that instead he has someone better to suggest, namely Toso Paic, as he was the most highly qualified policeman in our parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Milos Pajic was the one who told you that Toso Paic was the most highly qualified policeman or you obtained that information from other sources?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's what Milos Pajic told me. I wasn't bent on double-checking that information, nor did I have the means to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any affiliation between Milos Pajic and the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we fled to Serbia, I knew that Milos Pajic had become a member of the DB or that he had started working for the DB in a location close to Novi Sad. DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you aware of Milos Pajic and Toso Paic reporting on the security situation in Banija and Kordun to Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 4432, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, when the document comes up I'm going to give you a few moments to look at it and then I will ask you a few questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Same objection, with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness take his earphones off. Could you take your earphones off for a moment. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: This document talks about the witness. It came up when we did a search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how would I know? I mean, Mr. Jordash raises an objection and you say, as if I would have read it in a second, what it's all about. You say it's about this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't mean to imply that you would have known. That's the reason for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I have to rule on an objection, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question. I didn't have my headphones on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. I asked you if you have ever seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of your statement you speak of your establishment of a Serb cultural organisation called Sava Mrkalj. The "Srpski Glas" newspaper was launched by you and the other organisers of Sava Mrkalj according to this article, according to this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of 14 or 15 founders of the Serbian cultural society Sava Mrkalj and behind the launching of the first bulletin or newspaper in Cyrillic script in 40 or 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What was the aim of the publication of this article about war profiteering from the time when Milan Martic was minister in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not active in Sava Mrkalj at the time, so I truly wouldn't know either the sources or the reasons why the newspaper was published. I know the author because I took him over into the "Srpski Glas" editorial board after he had fled Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So if you were not aware of this report mentioning you, which was prepared by Dusan Orlovic, you were also, I presume, not aware that Franko Simatovic was receiving a copy of reports -- receiving a copy of this report prepared by DB operative Dusan Orlovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, the name "Dusan Orlovic" also appeared in a report which was shown to you by Mr. Jordash which is now MFI'd as D302. Can I ask you, did you yourself hold any position within any intelligence agency during the time you held your official government positions within the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Ever since I came of age, to this day, have I worked for any agency or service of anyone's of state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were there any other officials within the RSK whom you knew to be carrying out covert operations with intelligence organisations such as the DB?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who conducted covert operations, nor do I know of any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would like to note for the record that Dusan Orlovic is introduced by Mr. Stanisic to Mr. Milosevic in the Kula video P61 at minutes 9:02 to 10:13.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, in paragraph 85 of your statement, you say that during your meeting with Jovica Stanisic, Milan Martic, Milan Babic, and Bora Mijkalic [phoen] in 1994 there was nothing that indicated that Stanisic had any familiarity with Milan Babic or Milan Martic. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to tender into evidence 65 ter 4432, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P2998, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. The document is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please display Exhibit P631, page 3 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm showing you a transcript of a telephone conversation between Jovica Stanisic and Radovan Karadzic. This conversation took place in August 1991, nearly three years before the time you say you met Jovica Stanisic at that meeting. Can I direct your attention, please, to where Jovica Stanisic begins talking about Babic. He says that he was at Babic's for about two days fighting battles with him. Do you see that in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, would you agree that this demonstrates that there was a relationship between Stanisic and Babic already from 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with you because I wasn't present during the conversation. Babic never told me this. And this transcript is not something that I can confirm. I cannot comment on this. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, this is, of course, the answer you can -- to ask the witness to draw conclusions from a document which is unknown to him, not knowing about the authenticity, I mean, and so, therefore, I -- the answer is as you could expect from a witness who is carefully choosing his words. And let's try to elicit from the witness any information, any facts he has observed or -- rather than to ask him to draw conclusions of -- on documents which are unknown to him. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could the Court Officer please display Exhibit P636.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, according to evidence presented in this case, this intercept I'm showing you now is part of a series of conversations relating to the arrest of Milan Martic in Bosnia and the co-ordinated efforts of Milosevic, Stanisic, Karadzic, and Babic to have Milan Martic released. Could you read the first page to yourself, please. As you can see from this conversation, Stanisic and Karadzic are talking about the arrest of Milan Martic. Stanisic in fact informs Karadzic that Martic was arrested. At this point Karadzic only seems to know that Martic's men were arrested. As it turns out, Stanisic was correct, Martic was also arrested with his men. Were you aware of this incident when Milan Martic and a few of his men were arrested near Bosanska Krupa in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't read it through to the end, but I am aware of the incident. Would it be possible for me to read the latter part? I am aware of the incident, as I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You've never seen this transcript before, you are -- you do not know anything about telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Well, the only question that has been put to you, and which could have been put to you even without this document, was whether the witness was aware of the incident. Apparently he is. Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, do you know who was responsible for that arrest?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was arrested by, as we were told, by either the village guards or the police in Bosanska Krupa because the leaders were avoiding the area of Croatia and therefore crossed or travelled through Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Muslims, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you know how he was released?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. We were just informed that the intervention of people from Bosnia and Herzegovina and the army had been released. When I say Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean the Serbian SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm done with this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, you have presented yourself as having been a very close professional associate and personal friends of Mr. Babic. As you know, evidence presented by Milan Babic before this Tribunal in other cases is now admitted into evidence in this trial. We have 388 pages of testimony of Milan Babic from the Milosevic case, 75 pages from Krajisnik case, and 172 pages from the Martic case. In all that evidence, your name came up only twice, put to Babic by Mr. Milosevic in relation to your unfortunate arrest and mistreatment. Now, there was a stark contrast between the way you represent your close collaboration with Mr. Babic and his failure to bring up your name even once in these trials. Can you comment upon that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the last talk, when Babic said that he would Drag everybody else into the mud, we never saw each other again. And I suppose that he knew that I was against his reacting in that fashion. As regards my acquaintanceship and friendship with Dr. Babic, you could have checked that with people from the Krajina, the top leadership of the Krajina, of the SDS. All of them would have told you that Mile Bosnic was one of the closest associates and friends of Milan Babic's, especially as of the end of 1991 and the Vance Plan, that he came to see him officially and on friendly visits, that he spent nights in Slunj, et cetera, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw Mr. Babic before this conversation where he talked about coming to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not see each other again after that. And I found out from Dusan Vjestica that he had gone to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I would like to know about the meeting you had before that, so between the war time and when Mr. Babic went to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw each other quite frequently. I would go to see him in his aunt's flat at Altina [phoen], in Zemun. We tried to restore the work of the SDS because as a party we were also registered in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What time-period are you talking about, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period from my arrival, i.e., expulsion from the Krajina, onwards, meaning from August 1995 to the -- this last encounter. And it was not just I who attended those meetings. For a while we continued working in Belgrade as an exile government, a government in exile. We had our offices at 5 Terazije Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you aware that Milan Babic pled guilty to the charges which were the subject of the indictment against him?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I followed that via the media and TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So you may also be aware, then, are you, that due to the plea, although the Prosecution recommended imprisonment of no more than 11 years, the Trial Chamber was not bound by that recommendation, and so when Babic pled guilty, he was aware that he could be convicted to a life sentence as a result of his guilty plea? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that that is so, but I believe that he had some sort of an agreement with the Prosecution. It does strike me as unbelievable that he would admit to anything of that kind and then be given a life sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, the Chamber wonders how relevant it is, especially if you don't have much time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnic, yesterday when you were asked if you ever saw Mr. Stanisic after 1994, you said: "Not until I was called to testify to the events happening in the Krajina and Croatia for the Defence." Can you just clarify for us when was it then that you met Mr. Stanisic in relation to being called to testify in his defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where that meeting was?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This encounter took place in an office, where there were -- there was this attorney at law, a lady. It is on the Sava River, I believe. And there are some caravans that serve as lawyer's offices there. There I met on two occasions also with the gentleman from the Defence team. I don't know what the area name is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And you say that Mr. Stanisic was present at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was present at the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember which year that was?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that it was in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Stanisic any time between 2003 and coming to court to testify here?

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of that meeting, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE BOSNIC [Resumed]
